<STRUCT_0001>
Recall that we defined ringed spaces
in Sheaves, Section <REF_0001>.
Briefly, a ringed space is a pair <MATH_0001> consisting
of a topological space <MATH_0002> and a sheaf of rings <MATH_0003>.
A morphism of ringed spaces <MATH_0004>
is given by a continuous map <MATH_0005> and an <MATH_0006>-map of sheaves
of rings <MATH_0007>. You can
think of <MATH_0008> as a map <MATH_0009>, see
Sheaves, Definition <REF_0002> and
Lemma <REF_0003>.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
A good geometric example of this to keep in mind is
<MATH_0010>-manifolds and morphisms of
<MATH_0011>-manifolds. Namely, if <MATH_0012> is a
<MATH_0013>-manifold, then the sheaf <MATH_0014>
of smooth functions is a sheaf of rings on <MATH_0015>. And any
map <MATH_0016> of manifolds is smooth if and only if
for every local section <MATH_0017> of <MATH_0018>
the composition <MATH_0019> is a local section of <MATH_0020>.
Thus a smooth map <MATH_0021> gives rise in a natural way to a morphism
of ringed spaces

<STRUCT_0004><STRUCT_0005>
In algebraic geometry we study schemes. On a scheme the sheaf of rings
is not determined by an intrinsic property of the space.
The spectrum of a ring <MATH_0032>
(see Algebra, Section <REF_0006>) endowed
with a sheaf of rings constructed out of <MATH_0033> (see below),
will be our basic building block. It will turn out that
the stalks of <MATH_0034> on <MATH_0035> are the local
rings of <MATH_0036> at its primes. There are two reasons to introduce
locally ringed spaces in this setting: (1) There is in general
no mechanism that assigns to a continuous map of spectra a
map of the corresponding rings. This is why we add as an extra datum
the map <MATH_0037>. (2) If we consider morphisms
of these spectra in the category of ringed spaces, then the
maps on stalks may not be local homomorphisms. Since our
geometric intuition says it should we introduce locally ringed spaces
